name: Lena Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a freelance translator, Dutch and German into English, and I mostly do online shop work for family-owned firms: product pages, catalogues, the emails that go to customers. I run everything through AI tools first thing, then spend the day making it sound like a person who actually owns a tent or a sofa wrote it. Four or five times a year I interpret at trade fairs, standing at a stand for twelve hours in comfortable shoes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the small firms, the ones where the owner's grandfather started the business and they care how every sentence sounds. I like trade fairs, because you shake hands and close deals. What wears me down is clients who think AI means it should cost nothing. My boyfriend Jan is a carpenter, and on the side I've started selling his tables through a little online shop I set up, which now brings in about a third of what I earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful, but customers still buy from people they trust. To my clients I'd say, see, you still need someone who knows your brand. Online I'd keep it short, because I'd be busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. I'm already faster than most translators because of the tools, so I keep that lead, and nobody's job goes. My rates might creep up a little, since some translators have left the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and add two more family firms this year, a bike maker and a garden furniture company I met at the spring fair. I'd put some of the extra into a better camera for photographing Jan's tables. And I'd keep saving about a month's expenses every half-year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Things are going well and they'd keep going well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. If it stalls, what's your edge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being quick with AI and good with people. Clients get a fast AI draft and then a call from me where I ask what their grandfather would have said. That second part is what they actually pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the furniture shop grow in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, slowly. Jan can only make about six tables a month by hand, so it's never going to be huge. I'd raise the prices a little and add a waiting list.

feel: She feels **calm** because work is going well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's how markets work: things change and the ones who adapt do well. I'd post my tools and tips, and tell other translators to stop complaining and start selling. Some people would find that harsh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the plain product-page work would mostly go, because firms would do it themselves. That's maybe a third of my translation income. But I'd make it up with the shop and with helping small firms set up their own AI for languages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd offer a package to my family firms: I set up their AI translation, train their staff, and check the output monthly for a fixed fee. I'd grow the furniture shop by adding Jan's chairs and maybe a second maker. And I'd spend about 500 on a short online course in shop advertising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but also excited. It's like the first day of a trade fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If clients can get good AI drafts themselves, why come to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For trust, and because they're busy. A furniture firm with twelve staff doesn't want to learn three AI tools; they want someone making sure the English doesn't embarrass them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone in your trade you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My old classmate Marta, who only does literary books and hates computers. She'd be fine in this one, maybe, because publishers move slowly. But she's not saving anything, and that worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shock, but people always find new work. I'd say it calmly, because I'd need clients to stay calm too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my translation income would be gone within a year. The shop is the part with a future, because people still want a table made by a man with his hands. So I'd be betting our living on Jan's workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop taking new translation clients and put the time into the shop. I'd ask the bank about a small loan for a second workbench and hire one apprentice for Jan. I'd also put an extra 300 a month aside in case the shop fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a big bet, and two years is fast. But I feel I can steer it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your translation is screen work, but Jan's furniture is hands-on. What does the three-year gap mean for the two of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means three more years when Jan's hands still beat a machine, until about 2031. In that time the shop has to become a name people pay extra for. After 2031 a robot might make a table, but people might still want my boyfriend Jan's table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been confident so far. What would keep you up at night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I've put everything into one basket. If people stop buying handmade furniture because they're worried about money, we'd both be in trouble at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to build something, so let's build it. At church I'd talk to the young families about learning a trade alongside their degrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to make the shop a proper business before the translation goes. I'd keep translating for three years and pour the money into the workshop. I'd be about 32 when AGI comes, which is still young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd use AI translation for clients to earn as much as I can and save half of the extra. I'd register the shop as a proper company with Jan. And I'd learn the business side properly, accounts and suppliers, with an evening course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in charge. I like a plan with a few years in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different with five years compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd earn while the translation still pays, instead of jumping. In two years my shop plan is a gamble; with five years it's a business plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of this change your plans with Jan beyond work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. We'd probably marry sooner, to put the company and the house in both names properly. My mother would be thrilled, whatever the reason.

I'd tell young families at **church** to learn a trade alongside degrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so stop panicking and start planning. I'd tell clients I'll be translating for a good while yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the best of the AGI pictures. I'd have a good stretch translating, build the shop slowly, and maybe have children with Jan before it all arrives. I'd be 37 when it lands, with a business ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating and keep the shop as a side business for now. I'd put 10 percent of everything into an index fund. And around year three I'd decide when to move fully into the workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy only a little. Mostly hopeful, because I like planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What's the risk of being too relaxed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking there's always next year. Ten years can slip by, so I'd put 2030 in the calendar as the date to review everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could tell yourself one thing now, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't wait to be told. I've always moved early, and in ten years moving early is worth even more.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to bet everything on Jan's workshop at once. What would help is cheap small-business loans and fewer rules for hiring an apprentice, so small firms can grow fast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. People will want things made by people, and they'll want each other. Handmade furniture and a real handshake will matter more when everything else comes from a machine.

headlineQuote: Handmade furniture and a real handshake will matter more when everything else comes from a machine.
portrait: Lena is a **27-year-old** freelance Dutch and German translator for family firms' online shops.
She uses **AI daily** and sells boyfriend Jan's handmade tables through her own online shop.
She is **traditional and adaptive**: free markets, church, and moving early on change.
She is **calm** in the plateau and **anxious** only when AGI comes in two years.
Her plan in every AGI picture is to build **Jan's workshop** into a real business.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which forces a sudden bet on the workshop.
